rejected.title: Australians in the Pacific war
card: Japan entered the war in December 1941 and moved quickly through South-East Asia. Many Australian soldiers were sent to defend Malaya and Singapore, a British base.
Fall of Singapore
Singapore surrendered to Japan in February 1942. About 15,000 Australians were among the many thousands of Allied troops taken prisoner.
Prisoners of war
Prisoners of war (POWs) were held in camps and forced to work, such as on the Thai-Burma railway. Many died from disease, hunger and harsh treatment.
Kokoda Track

In 1942 Japanese troops landed on the north coast of Papua and tried to cross the Owen Stanley Range towards Port Moresby. Australian troops fought them along the Kokoda Track in jungle and mud, and forced them to retreat.
rejected.remember: Singapore's fall in 1942 led to Australians being held as POWs. On the Kokoda Track, Australians turned back the Japanese advance.

a.q: What happened to many Australian soldiers after Singapore fell in 1942?
opts: They were taken prisoner by Japan
They were sent home to defend Darwin
They were moved to fight in Europe
They were sent along the Kokoda Track
a.why: Singapore surrendered in February 1942, and about 15,000 Australians became prisoners of war. The Kokoda Track fighting was a separate campaign in Papua, fought later in 1942.
a.clue: Singapore surrendered, so the soldiers there could not keep fighting.

b.q: Why was the fighting on the Kokoda Track important to Australia in 1942?
opts: Australians stopped Japan's advance towards Port Moresby
Australians recaptured Singapore from Japan
Australians freed the prisoners on the Thai-Burma railway
Australians ended the war in the Pacific
b.why: Japanese troops were trying to cross the Owen Stanley Range towards Port Moresby, and Australian troops forced them to retreat. Singapore stayed in Japanese hands and the prisoners were not freed by this fighting.
b.clue: Think about where the Japanese troops were trying to go.

wants.brief: A map of Papua New Guinea showing the Kokoda Track from the north coast near Buna to Port Moresby, crossing the Owen Stanley Range, with Port Moresby and Kokoda labelled.
wants.why: It shows where the track ran and why Port Moresby was the Japanese target.

version.title: Australians in the Pacific war
card: In December 1941 Japan attacked across South-East Asia. Thousands of Australian soldiers were in Malaya and Singapore, helping Britain defend its main base in the region.
Fall of Singapore
Japanese forces pushed south through Malaya, and Singapore surrendered in February 1942. About 15,000 Australians were taken prisoner there.
Prisoners of war

Prisoners of war (POWs) were held until the war ended in 1945, and many were forced to build the Thai-Burma railway. About a third of the Australians held by Japan died, from disease, hunger and brutal treatment.
Kokoda Track

In July 1942 Japanese troops landed on Papua's north coast to cross the Owen Stanley Range by the Kokoda Track and take Port Moresby, a base close to northern Australia. Fighting in jungle and mud, Australians stopped them short of Port Moresby and from late September pushed them back over the range.
version.remember: Singapore's fall left thousands of Australians as prisoners of war. On the Kokoda Track, Australians stopped Japan short of Port Moresby.

a.q: Why did about 15,000 Australians become prisoners of war in February 1942?
opts: Singapore, the base they were defending, surrendered
Japan defeated them on the Kokoda Track in Papua
They were captured working on the Thai-Burma railway
Their troopships were sunk while sailing to Malaya
a.why: The Australians in Singapore were taken prisoner when it surrendered to Japan in February 1942. The Kokoda Track fighting began later, in July 1942, and there Australians pushed the Japanese back. The railway was built by prisoners after they were captured.
a.clue: Where were thousands of Australian soldiers when Japan attacked?

b.q: A 1942 diary by an Australian soldier describes thick jungle, steep mud, a mountain range, and the enemy now falling back towards the north coast. Which part of the Pacific war does it describe?
opts: The Kokoda Track campaign in Papua
The defence of Singapore in 1942
Work on the Thai-Burma railway
The fighting retreat through Malaya
b.why: On the Kokoda Track, Australians fought in jungle and mud on Papua's mountains and pushed the Japanese back towards the north coast. The railway also ran through jungle, but the men there were prisoners, not soldiers pushing an enemy back. In Malaya and Singapore the Australians were the ones forced back.
b.clue: In which fighting were the Australians the side moving forward?

wants.brief: A simple map of Papua and the far north of Australia. It shows the north coast of Papua with Buna and Gona, the village of Kokoda, the Owen Stanley Range, the Kokoda Track as a line from Kokoda over the range to Port Moresby on the south coast, and the tip of Cape York across the sea, labelled Australia.
wants.why: It shows where the track ran and how close Port Moresby was to Australia.
